title: The vowels
hookLine: hey and heyyyy are different messages; Pali writes the stretch into the word
tomorrow: why does dhamma have an h that's so hard to hear?

cards: In a text, hey and heyyyy are not the same message. Nobody taught you that rule. You just know a stretched sound is carrying something a short one isn't.
Pali writes the stretch into the spelling. Some vowels are short, clipped. Some are long, held.
That's why a chant leans on some sounds and hurries past others. It isn't a temple's style. It's the words themselves.

teach.b: Here they are. Three short ones: a, said like the u in but; i, like the i in pin; u, like the u in put.
Three long ones, the same sounds held: a, like father; i, like machine; u, like rule. In roman letters, the long ones wear a little bar on top.

teach.h: E AND O: LONG, WITH A CATCH.
teach.b: Then e, as in they, and o, as in go, which count as long, with one catch: before a double consonant they go short, as in metta. Teachers say a long vowel takes about twice the time of a short one.
Yesterday's word shows it: Pali is a long a, then a short i. Dhamma is two short a's, quick and open.
Nibbana goes short, long, short. Get the lengths right and a chant keeps its shape, because the old verses are built on a pattern of long and short. Stretch everything and the pattern smears.
Open vowels, each given its own time.

how: Theravada chanting books often print the Pali in roman letters with marks over the long vowels, and new chanters learn the lengths by ear, chanting along with monks and longtime lay chanters.

o: the open sounds a chant is built on, short and long
the high notes a lead chanter sings on their own
the silent letters chanters skip when going fast

p: the long a, as in father
the short a, like the u in but
the long i, as in machine
an e gone short before a double t

s: in a chant, every vowel is stretched slow and even
short ones stay short and long ones are held; that pattern is the chant's rhythm.
a bar over a letter, as in ā, marks a long vowel
in roman letters, ā, ī and ū are the long ones, held about twice as long, teachers say.
e and o are long in every Pali word
they count as long, but go short before a double consonant, as in metta.

games.q: your chant sheet has no bars over any letters, and you reach the word nibbana. which a do you hold?
o: the middle one: nibbana goes short, long, short, marked or not.
all three: long vowels are what make a chant sound right.
none: the bars are decoration for scholars, so clip them all.
games.why: the bar only shows the length; the length belongs to the word. nibbana holds its middle a, whether the sheet marks it or not.

practice: Say each vowel slowly, out loud, one to a breath: a, then aa; i, then ee; u, then oo; then e, and o. Let the short ones stay short and give the long ones their full time, then rest in the quiet after the last o.

wordCard.voice: The vowels. Short a, i and u; long a, i and u; and e and o. The open floor every chant stands on.

orig.s: अ आ इ ई उ ऊ ए ओ
orig.say: a, AA, i, EE, u, OO, ay, oh
orig.note: the Pali vowels in Devanagari letters: short a, long ā, short i, long ī, short u, long ū, then e and o.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: open vowels, where short stays short and long gets its time. Two days into Pali.
